chapter_note.about: A data cube lets you view the same facts at many levels of detail. This chapter covers the levels of a dimension (concept hierarchies), the operations that move between levels (roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice), how many cuboids and cells a cube has, and how measures such as SUM, AVG and MEDIAN combine when you go up a level. GATE DA asks you to name the operation that connects two views, to count cuboids with hierarchies, or to say what can be computed from stored values.
chapter_note.simple: Picture a spreadsheet of sales that you can zoom, like a map. Zoomed in you see every shop and every day; zoomed out you see only states and years. Zooming out adds the numbers up, and zooming in splits them back. The zoom levels are the hierarchy, and every mix of levels is one view (a cuboid) of the data. Adding up works easily for totals and counts, but averages need the number of items behind them, and a middle value needs all the raw numbers. The exam asks you to name the zoom move, count the views, or combine numbers correctly.

cards.title: Concept hierarchies
cards.simple: Think of your home address. You live in a flat, which is in a city, which is in a state, which is in a country. Each step up is a bigger box that holds the smaller ones. A concept hierarchy is the same idea for the data in a warehouse: the levels of one way of looking at the data, from very detailed to very general. Every small thing has exactly one bigger thing it belongs to, so you can add up the small things to get the big thing's total. At the very top there is one box called ALL that means 'everything together'. In exam words: the levels of a dimension are ordered from specific to general (City, State, Country), each child value has one parent value, and ALL is the single top value.
cards.idea: A **concept hierarchy** orders the levels of one dimension from specific to general, such as City, State, Country. Each value at a lower level belongs to exactly **one** value at the level above. Above the top real level sits **ALL**, a single value that means 'ignore this dimension'.
cards.definition:
A dimension has levels $L_1 < L_2 < \dots < L_m$, from finest to coarsest.

- Every value at level $L_i$ has exactly one parent value at level $L_{i+1}$ (a many-to-one link).
- ALL is one extra top value above $L_m$.
- Some dimensions have a partial order (Day $\to$ Week and Day $\to$ Month $\to$ Year): then a level can have more than one coarser level above it.
cards.intuition_full: A warehouse stores facts at the finest level it can: one sale in one city on one day. Analysts rarely want that detail, so they need a map from fine to coarse. The hierarchy is that map. Because each city has only one state, you can sum city sales into state sales without counting anything twice. If a value had two parents, a roll-up would double-count it, which is why the many-to-one rule is part of the definition. ALL is the coarsest possible level: one value, the grand total. It also matters for counting cuboids later, since leaving a dimension out of a group-by is the same as grouping at ALL. Some hierarchies are not a single chain. Days roll up to months and also to weeks, but a week can straddle two months, so Week and Month are side-by-side levels rather than one above the other.

examples.setup: Sales are recorded for four cities: Mumbai, Pune, Chennai, Madurai. Build the location hierarchy bottom-up.
steps: The facts are stored per city: Mumbai, Pune, Chennai, Madurai. City is the finest level of the location dimension.
Mumbai and Pune belong to Maharashtra. Chennai and Madurai belong to Tamil Nadu. State is the next level up.
Both states belong to India. Country is the level above State.
Read the levels from specific to general: City, State, Country. Each city has exactly one state and each state exactly one country.
Above Country is one more value, ALL, which means 'everything together'. It stands for ignoring the dimension.
examples.answer: City (finest) → State → Country → ALL (coarsest).

examples.setup: A time dimension has the levels Day, Week, Month and Year. Days roll up to weeks, and days roll up to months, and months roll up to years. Can Week roll up to Month?
steps: Test the rule: every child value must have exactly one parent value at the next level.
Day 2025-01-01 → Month January has one parent. Day → Week also has one parent.
Take the week 29 Dec to 4 Jan. Its days lie in two different months, December and January. The week has two possible parents.
So Week does not roll up to Month. Day has two separate paths: Day → Week and Day → Month → Year.
Such a hierarchy is a partial order, not a chain. This matters when counting cuboids.
examples.answer: No. Week and Month are side-by-side levels; both sit above Day.

examples.setup: Two different towns are both called Aurangabad: one in Maharashtra, one in Bihar. A table stores city names only. What goes wrong when you roll up?
steps: Group by the city name 'Aurangabad': both towns fall into one group, say sales 30 (Maharashtra) and 20 (Bihar) merge into 50.
The parent is also unknown: is that group in Maharashtra or Bihar?
A city value must identify its parent. Use (State, City) as the key, or give each city an id.
Then roll-up gives Maharashtra 30 and Bihar 20 from these two towns.
examples.answer: The name alone is ambiguous. Identify a city by (State, City), so every child has one parent.

cards.title: Roll-up and drill-down
cards.simple: Think of a map app. Zoomed in, you see every street. Zoom out and the streets merge into neighbourhoods, then into the city. Zooming out is roll-up: you add things up and see fewer, bigger pieces. Zooming in is drill-down: the big piece splits back into its smaller pieces. Slicing is different. You stay at the same zoom level and just look at part of the map, like only one neighbourhood. In exam words: roll-up goes to a coarser level or drops a dimension, drill-down goes to a finer level, and slice and dice select values without changing any level.
cards.idea: **Roll-up** moves to a coarser level (Item to Type) and adds up the children. **Drill-down** moves to a finer level and splits the totals back into details. **Slice and dice** keep the levels and only choose which values to show. **Pivot** rotates the view.
cards.definition:
Compare the old and new level of each dimension.

- Level goes up (finer to coarser) or the dimension is dropped to ALL: **roll-up**. The cube gets smaller.
- Level goes down (coarser to finer): **drill-down**. The cube gets bigger.
- Same levels, fewer values: **slice** (one value of one dimension) or **dice** (several values on two or more dimensions).
- Same data, axes swapped: **pivot (rotate)**.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the hierarchy as a staircase. Roll-up climbs one step, using the aggregate function to merge the children into their parent. Drill-down descends one step and needs the finer data (or a stored finer cuboid) to show the pieces again. Neither changes the facts, only the level at which you view them. The shape of the result gives it away: if the view has fewer cells, it was rolled up. Slice and dice are more like a filter. The levels are untouched, so the cell count shrinks only because some values are hidden. In exam questions the trick is almost always to name the levels before and after, and to compare them using the hierarchy order. If two dimensions change in opposite directions, the view change is a drill-down on one dimension combined with a roll-up on another.

examples.setup: Sales in thousand rupees by Item: Laptop 70, Phone 50, Pen 5, Notebook 15. Items belong to types: Laptop and Phone are Tech; Pen and Notebook are Office.
steps: The cube is at the Item level: Laptop 70, Phone 50, Pen 5, Notebook 15.
Roll-up from Item to Type: add the children. Tech = 70 + 50 = 120 and Office = 5 + 15 = 20. Four rows become two.
Drill-down from Type back to Item: Tech splits into Laptop 70 and Phone 50. Two rows become four.
Slice Type = Tech: keep only the Laptop and Phone rows. The level is still Item, only some values remain.
So roll-up is coarser and smaller, drill-down is finer and bigger, and slice keeps the level.
examples.answer: Roll-up: Tech 120, Office 20. Drill-down restores the 4 item rows. Slice keeps Laptop and Phone.

cards.title: Cuboid count with hierarchies
cards.simple: Imagine ordering a thali where you choose one option from each section. In the first section you may pick Day, Month or Year, or skip that section (that is ALL). In the second you pick Item or Type, or skip. In the third you pick Store or skip. Every different combination of choices is a different 'cuboid', which is one way of grouping the data. To count the combinations you multiply the number of choices in each section. A section with 3 levels has 3 plus 1 skip option, so 4 choices. In exam words: a dimension with L levels offers L + 1 choices including ALL, and the number of cuboids is the product of (L + 1) over all dimensions.
cards.idea: A **cuboid** is one way to group the cube: pick one level (or ALL) for every dimension. A dimension with $L$ levels gives $L+1$ choices. The number of cuboids is the **product** of these choices, not $2^n$.
cards.definition:
For $n$ dimensions with $L_1, L_2, \dots, L_n$ levels (not counting ALL):

$$\text{cuboids}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(L_i+1)$$

- $L_i+1$ counts the $L_i$ levels plus ALL.
- With one level per dimension every factor is 2, which gives the familiar $2^n$.
- For a partial order, count every level once: a dimension with 4 levels still gives 5 choices.
cards.intuition_full: A cuboid is defined by a group-by: for each dimension you either group at one particular level or leave the dimension out. Leaving it out is the same as grouping at ALL, so each dimension offers one choice per real level plus one for ALL. The choices for different dimensions are independent, so the counts multiply, the same way 3 shirts and 2 trousers give 6 outfits. The base cuboid uses the finest level of every dimension; the apex uses ALL everywhere and is a single grand total. The classic formula 2^n only counts the case where every dimension has a single level, so it undercounts as soon as a dimension has a hierarchy. For a partial order such as Day to Week and Day to Month to Year, one group-by picks only one level per dimension, so Week and Month are two separate options and each still counts once.

examples.setup: A cube has three dimensions. Time has the levels Day, Month, Year. Product has Item, Type. Store has just Store. How many cuboids does it have?
steps: Time has 3 levels. A cuboid shows Time at Day, Month or Year, or drops it (ALL): 3 + 1 = 4 choices.
Product has 2 levels: Item, Type, or ALL: 2 + 1 = 3 choices.
Store has 1 level: Store, or ALL: 1 + 1 = 2 choices.
A cuboid takes one choice per dimension, for example (Month, Type, ALL). Every combination is a different cuboid: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
Without hierarchies the count would be 2^3 = 8. Hierarchies multiply the choices instead.
examples.answer: 24 cuboids.

examples.setup: A cube has four dimensions with 1, 2, 2 and 3 levels (not counting ALL). How many cuboids are there? How many of them use an actual level (no ALL) in every dimension?
steps: Choices per dimension: 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 1 = 3, 2 + 1 = 3, 3 + 1 = 4.
Total cuboids = 2 × 3 × 3 × 4 = 72.
No ALL anywhere: each dimension must choose a real level, so the factors are 1, 2, 2, 3. That gives 1 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.
The apex cuboid (ALL in every dimension) is exactly one of the 72.
Trap avoided: 2^4 = 16 would be wrong, because the dimensions have hierarchies.
examples.answer: 72 cuboids in all; 12 of them have no ALL.

examples.setup: Time has the levels Day, Week, Month, Year, where Day → Week and Day → Month → Year. Customer has one level. How many cuboids?
steps: Time has 4 distinct levels. A group-by uses only one level of a dimension, so Week and Month are two separate choices.
Time choices: 4 + 1 = 5 (Day, Week, Month, Year, ALL).
Customer choices: 1 + 1 = 2.
examples.answer: 10 cuboids.

The apex cuboid (ALL in all dimensions) is always counted.
In a partial order, count each level once; levels that are not comparable are separate choices.
If the question says the levels include ALL already, do not add 1 again.

cards.title: Cells in a cuboid
cards.simple: A cuboid is a table, and its cells are the boxes in the table. Say you group sales by shirt type (3 kinds), by year (2 years) and by region (2 regions). That makes 3 rows by 2 columns for each region, and there are 2 regions, so 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 boxes. You count the boxes by multiplying how many values each chosen level has. If a dimension is left out (ALL), it has just one value, so it multiplies by 1. In exam words: the number of cells in a dense cuboid is the product of the number of distinct values at the chosen level of each dimension, and ALL contributes 1.
cards.idea: The **cells** of a cuboid are all combinations of one value per dimension, at the chosen levels. Count them by **multiplying** the number of distinct values at each chosen level. A dimension at ALL contributes **1**.
cards.definition:
For a dense cuboid with levels $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$ and $|\ell_i|$ distinct values at the chosen level of dimension $i$:

$$\text{cells}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}|\ell_i|$$

- $|\text{ALL}|=1$.
- Dense means every combination exists. A real (sparse) cube has at most as many non-empty cells as it has fact rows.
- Total cells over all cuboids factor by dimension: $\prod_i\bigl(1+\sum_{\ell\in i}|\ell|\bigr)$.
cards.intuition_full: A cell is a spot in the grid where you can store one aggregate, such as the total sales for (Type A, 2023, East). The grid has one axis per dimension, and the length of an axis is the number of values at the level you chose. The number of grid spots is the product of the axis lengths, like the number of squares in a multi-layer chessboard. A finer level means a longer axis, so the base cuboid (finest everywhere) is the biggest. ALL is an axis of length 1: a single position that holds the grand total for that dimension. Summing the cells over every cuboid is easier by dimension: the choices of different dimensions are independent, so the total factors into one bracket per dimension, with a 1 for ALL and then each level's size.

cards.title: Measure categories
cards.simple: Say two friends each count the money in their piggy bank, and you want the total for both. Easy: add the two totals. You can also find the richest of the two by comparing their biggest coins. But the 'typical' coin value is trickier. You cannot just average the two averages, because one friend may have many more coins. You need each friend's total and coin count. And the middle coin of everyone together cannot be found from each friend's middle coin at all; you need all the coins. In exam words: distributive measures (SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX) combine directly, algebraic ones (AVG, standard deviation) combine from a few stored numbers, and holistic ones (MEDIAN, MODE, RANK) need the raw data.
cards.idea: A cube combines partial results, so it matters how a measure combines. **Distributive**: combine the pieces' results with a simple function (SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX). **Algebraic**: needs a fixed few pieces, such as (sum, count) for AVG. **Holistic**: no fixed-size summary works (MEDIAN, MODE, RANK).
cards.definition:
Split the data into partitions and compute the measure on each.

- **Distributive**: $F(\text{all})=G(F(\text{part}_1),F(\text{part}_2),\dots)$ for a simple combining function $G$ (for SUM, MIN, MAX it is $F$ itself; for COUNT it is SUM). Examples: SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX.
- **Algebraic**: $F(\text{all})$ is a function of a fixed number of distributive results. AVG from (SUM, COUNT); variance from (COUNT, SUM, SUM of squares).
- **Holistic**: there is no fixed-size summary per partition that gives $F(\text{all})$. Examples: MEDIAN, MODE, RANK.
cards.intuition_full: Think about what the cube stores. If each cell stores one number per measure, the roll-up must rebuild the parent from the children's numbers alone. For SUM that works because sums add. For MAX it works because the biggest of the pieces' maxima is the overall max. AVG fails if you store only the average: the parent average depends on how many values each child had, so you must also store the count. Two numbers are enough, so AVG is algebraic. Standard deviation needs three: count, sum and sum of squares. MEDIAN fails for every fixed-size summary: the middle of everything depends on the exact positions of all the values, so you must keep the raw data (or a sketch that is only approximate). That is what holistic means. A quick test: could someone with only the stored numbers of each piece compute the answer for the union?

examples.setup: Split the data 1, 2, 4, 5, 9 into P1 = {2, 4, 9} and P2 = {1, 5}. Try to rebuild SUM, MAX, AVG and MEDIAN of the whole from the pieces.
steps: Whole data: 1, 2, 4, 5, 9. True SUM = 21, MAX = 9, AVG = 21/5 = 4.2, MEDIAN = 4.
SUM: the partial sums are 15 and 6. Combine: 15 + 6 = 21, equal to the true sum. Distributive.
MAX: the partial maxima are 9 and 5. Combine: max(9, 5) = 9, the true max. Distributive.
AVG: partial averages 5 and 3 give (5 + 3)/2 = 4, not 4.2. But the pairs (sum, count) = (15, 3) and (6, 2) give (15 + 6)/(3 + 2) = 4.2. Algebraic.
MEDIAN: partial medians 4 and 3 cannot give the true median 4 (averaging them gives 3.5). No fixed-size summary works. Holistic.
examples.answer: SUM and MAX are distributive, AVG is algebraic, MEDIAN is holistic.

examples.setup: Each cell stores (count, sum, sum of squares) of its values. Which of COUNT, SUM, AVG, VARIANCE, MEDIAN and MAX can be computed exactly for the union of cells?
steps: COUNT and SUM are the stored count and sum: add them across cells.
AVG = total sum / total count: computable.
VARIANCE = (sum of squares)/count − (mean)²: computable from the three stored numbers.
MAX is not among the stored numbers and cannot be recovered from them.
MEDIAN needs the exact positions of the values: not recoverable.
examples.answer: COUNT, SUM, AVG and VARIANCE yes; MAX and MEDIAN no.

examples.setup: Two stores report profit margin = profit / sales. Store 1: profit 50 on sales 100 (50%). Store 2: profit 80 on sales 400 (20%). What is the combined margin? Can margins simply be averaged?
steps: Average the two margins: (50% + 20%)/2 = 35%. This is wrong.
Add the underlying measures first: profit 50 + 80 = 130, sales 100 + 400 = 500.
Combined margin = 130 / 500 = 26%.
A ratio is non-additive. Store profit and sales (both additive) and divide at the end.

how: Split the data in two and try to rebuild the answer from the pieces' results alone.

cards.title: Computing measures from partial aggregates
cards.simple: Say two classes sent you only three numbers each about their test marks: how many students, the total of all marks, and the total of every mark squared. You never see the individual marks. Can you still work out the average and how spread out the marks are for both classes together? Yes. Add the counts, add the totals and add the squared totals. The average is the total divided by the count. The spread comes from a small formula using the squared totals. In exam words: AVG = total sum / total count, and variance = (sum of squares)/n − mean², where n, the sum and the sum of squares are added across cells.
cards.idea: Algebraic measures roll up if each cell stores a few **distributive pieces**. AVG needs the **count and sum**. Variance needs the count, the sum and the **sum of squares**. Add each piece across cells, then compute the measure once at the end.
cards.definition:
With $n=\sum n_i$, $S=\sum s_i$ and $Q=\sum q_i$ added over the cells:

$$\text{AVG}=\frac{S}{n},\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{Q}{n}-\left(\frac{S}{n}\right)^2$$

- $n_i$, $s_i$, $q_i$ are the count, sum and sum of squares of cell $i$.
- This is the population variance. The sample variance is $\dfrac{Q-S^2/n}{n-1}$.
cards.intuition_full: The trick is to store things that add. A mean does not add, but the pair (sum, count) does. A variance does not add either, but (count, sum, sum of squares) does. Once the three numbers are added across cells, the formulas turn them back into the measure for the combined data. The variance formula comes from expanding the definition: the mean of the squared deviations equals the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean, E[x²] − (E[x])². Each of the two terms can be rebuilt from Q, S and n. That is why storing only the variance of each cell is not enough: you could not combine two variances without also knowing the means and counts. The standard deviation is the square root of the final variance, computed last, because square roots do not add.

examples.setup: Cell X summarises the values 2, 4, 9 and cell Y summarises 1, 5. Only the summaries (n, sum, sum of squares) are stored: X = (3, 15, 101), Y = (2, 6, 26). Find the mean and population variance of the combined data.
steps: X = (3, 15, 101) and Y = (2, 6, 26). The raw values are not available, only these three numbers each.
Add the pieces: n = 3 + 2 = 5, sum = 15 + 6 = 21, sum of squares = 101 + 26 = 127.
Mean of squares = 127 / 5 = 25.4.
examples.answer: Mean 4.2, population variance 7.76.

examples.setup: Partition P1 has 6 values with average 25. Partition P2 has 4 values with average 40. What is the average of all 10 values?
steps: Rebuild the sums: P1 sum = 6 × 25 = 150, P2 sum = 4 × 40 = 160.
Total sum = 310, total count = 10.
Trap avoided: (25 + 40) / 2 = 32.5 ignores that P1 has more values.

examples.setup: Using the combined summary (n, S, Q) = (5, 21, 127) from the first example, find the SAMPLE variance.
steps: Sum of squared deviations = Q − S² / n = 127 − 441 / 5 = 127 − 88.2 = 38.8.
Sample variance divides by n − 1 = 4: 38.8 / 4 = 9.7.
The population variance divided the same 38.8 by n = 5 and gave 7.76.
examples.answer: 9.7 (sample) against 7.76 (population).

cards.title: Aggregating along a hierarchy
cards.simple: Say three shops in one town report 'we sold 4 items at an average price of 50', '1 item at 80' and '5 items at 30'. What is the town's average price? Do not add 50, 80 and 30 and divide by 3, because the shop that sold only one item would count as much as the shop that sold five. Turn each average back into a total (4 times 50 and so on), add the totals, and divide by the total number of items sold. Sums and biggest values are easier: just add the sums, or take the biggest of the biggest. In exam words: distributive measures roll up directly, averages roll up weighted by counts (or from sum and count), and medians cannot be rolled up without the raw data.
cards.idea: Going up a hierarchy, **SUM, COUNT, MIN and MAX** combine directly (sums add, counts add, the largest of the maxima wins). An **average** must be weighted by the counts. A **median** cannot be rebuilt from the children's medians; it needs the raw data.
cards.definition:
For a parent $P$ with children $c=1..k$ having counts $n_c$, sums $s_c$, averages $a_c=s_c/n_c$:

- $\text{SUM}_P=\sum s_c$, $\text{COUNT}_P=\sum n_c$, $\text{MAX}_P=\max_c \text{MAX}_c$.
- $\text{AVG}_P=\dfrac{\sum n_c a_c}{\sum n_c}$, a weighted average with weights $n_c$.
- $\text{MEDIAN}_P$ has no formula in the children's medians.
cards.intuition_full: A parent value is the union of its children's data, so the question is always: what must each child tell me so that I can answer for the union? For a sum, one number per child is enough. For an average, the child's average alone hides how many values it stands for, so a big child must pull the parent average more than a small one. That is exactly what weighting by the count does. It is the same as recovering each child's total (count × average), adding the totals, and dividing by the total count. The weights matter at every level: when going from state to country, use the state counts, not the number of cities. If you store (sum, count) at every level, the arithmetic is always the same simple division, and no information is lost on the way up.

examples.setup: Three cities in a state hold (count, average sale): Pune (4, 50), Nashik (1, 80), Nagpur (5, 30). Find the state's average sale.
steps: Each city cell holds (count, average): Pune (4, 50), Nashik (1, 80), Nagpur (5, 30). The state needs the average over all sales.
Rebuild each city's total: 4 × 50 = 200, 1 × 80 = 80, 5 × 30 = 150.
Add the totals and the counts: sum = 200 + 80 + 150 = 430, count = 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.
State average = 430 / 10 = 43.
The shortcut (50 + 80 + 30) / 3 = 53.33 is wrong: it treats Nashik's single sale like Pune's four.

examples.answer: SUM 430, COUNT 10, MAX 90, AVG 43; the median cannot be found from city values.

steps: The unweighted average (43 + 20) / 2 = 31.5 is wrong. The weights are the state counts at every level.

how: Write (count, sum) for every child; if only the average is given, sum = count × average.
For SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX: apply the same function to the children's values.
For AVG: total sum / total count.
For MEDIAN or MODE: you need the raw data, so say it cannot be derived.
cards.mistake: Averaging the children's averages without weights, or assuming MEDIAN rolls up like MAX. The simple mean of the children is right only if every child has the same count.
edge_cases: If all children have equal counts, the plain mean of the children's averages is correct.
A child with count 0 contributes nothing; skip it.
MIN and MAX roll up directly even when the counts differ.
Weights are counts of facts, not counts of child cells.

example.setup: Three cities in a state hold (count, average sale): Pune (4, 50), Nashik (1, 80), Nagpur (5, 30). Find the state's average sale.
steps: Each city cell holds (count, average): Pune (4, 50), Nashik (1, 80), Nagpur (5, 30). The state needs the average over all sales.
Rebuild each city's total: 4 × 50 = 200, 1 × 80 = 80, 5 × 30 = 150.
Add the totals and the counts: sum = 200 + 80 + 150 = 430, count = 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.
State average = 430 / 10 = 43.
The shortcut (50 + 80 + 30) / 3 = 53.33 is wrong: it treats Nashik's single sale like Pune's four.

cards.what: Going up a hierarchy, **SUM, COUNT, MIN and MAX** combine directly (sums add, counts add, the largest of the maxima wins). An **average** must be weighted by the counts. A **median** cannot be rebuilt from the children's medians; it needs the raw data.
cards.what_full:
Going up a hierarchy, **SUM, COUNT, MIN and MAX** combine directly (sums add, counts add, the largest of the maxima wins). An **average** must be weighted by the counts. A **median** cannot be rebuilt from the children's medians; it needs the raw data.

For a parent $P$ with children $c=1..k$ having counts $n_c$, sums $s_c$, averages $a_c=s_c/n_c$:

- $\text{SUM}_P=\sum s_c$, $\text{COUNT}_P=\sum n_c$, $\text{MAX}_P=\max_c \text{MAX}_c$.
- $\text{AVG}_P=\dfrac{\sum n_c a_c}{\sum n_c}$, a weighted average with weights $n_c$.
- $\text{MEDIAN}_P$ has no formula in the children's medians.

**Worked example.** Three cities in a state hold (count, average sale): Pune (4, 50), Nashik (1, 80), Nagpur (5, 30). Find the state's average sale.

1. Each city cell holds (count, average): Pune (4, 50), Nashik (1, 80), Nagpur (5, 30). The state needs the average over all sales.
2. Rebuild each city's total: 4 × 50 = 200, 1 × 80 = 80, 5 × 30 = 150.
3. Add the totals and the counts: sum = 200 + 80 + 150 = 430, count = 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.
4. State average = 430 / 10 = 43.
5. The shortcut (50 + 80 + 30) / 3 = 53.33 is wrong: it treats Nashik's single sale like Pune's four.

**Answer:** 43.

Cubes pre-aggregate at each level, and a wrong roll-up gives a wrong answer silently. In GATE: DA gives (count, average) pairs for a few cells and asks for the parent average, or asks which measures can be derived at the coarser level.

cards.trap: Averaging the children's averages without weights, or assuming MEDIAN rolls up like MAX. The simple mean of the children is right only if every child has the same count.

cards.title: Measures versus dimension attributes
cards.simple: Look at one line of a shop bill: the date, the product name, the town, how many were sold and the amount. Some columns tell you the situation: when, what, where. You use those to group the bills, like 'all bills in Pune'. Other columns are numbers you add up: how many, how much money. Those are the things you measure. The groups come from the first kind, the totals come from the second. A percentage like a discount is a number too, but adding up percentages of different bills makes no sense, so it needs care. In exam words: dimension attributes describe context and are used to group and filter; measures are numeric facts that are aggregated.
cards.idea: A **measure** is a number you aggregate (sale amount, quantity). A **dimension attribute** describes context (date, product, city) and is used to **group** and filter. The fact table holds the measures plus keys that point to the dimensions.
cards.definition:
- **Measure**: a numeric fact stored in the fact table, aggregated with SUM, COUNT, AVG, and so on.
- **Dimension attribute**: a descriptive value (a level of a hierarchy, such as month or city) used in GROUP BY and WHERE.
- Test: *would I add this column up across rows?* If yes it is a measure. If I would group by it, it is a dimension attribute.
- Additivity: **additive** measures add across every dimension; **semi-additive** ones (balances) do not add across time; **non-additive** ones (ratios, prices) never add.
cards.intuition_full: A data cube answers questions of the form 'total of this number, broken down by those descriptions'. The number is the measure; the descriptions are the dimension attributes. Mixing them up produces nonsense, like summing dates or grouping by amount. The fact table stores one row per event with the numeric facts and keys; the dimension tables hold the descriptions and the hierarchies. Measures differ in how safely they add. Quantity and revenue add across everything. An account balance adds across accounts at one date, but adding balances across months is meaningless, so it is semi-additive. A unit price or a percentage never adds; store the pieces you can add (revenue and quantity) and divide at the end, which is the same logic as the weighted average of the previous cards.

examples.setup: One sale row: date 14 Mar, product Laptop, city Pune, quantity 2, amount 70000, discount 10 (percent). Which columns are dimension attributes and which are measures?
steps: One sale: date 14 Mar, product Laptop, city Pune, quantity 2, amount 70000, discount 10 percent.
Ask of each column: do I add it up, or do I group by it? Date, product and city are used to group and filter. They describe context: dimension attributes.
Quantity and amount are numbers I add across rows (total amount by city, total quantity by month). They are measures, and additive ones.
Discount percent is a number too, but adding discount percentages from different bills is meaningless. It is a non-additive measure.
Check by trying: SUM(amount) grouped by city makes sense. SUM(date) does not. So group-by columns are dimensions, aggregated numbers are measures.
examples.answer: Dimensions: date, product, city. Measures: quantity and amount (additive), discount percent (non-additive).

examples.setup: A fact table has the columns order_id, customer_key, date_key, product_key, units, unit_price and revenue = units × unit_price. Two rows: (units 2, unit_price 500, revenue 1000) and (units 3, unit_price 400, revenue 1200). Classify the columns and say which measures add.
steps: customer_key, date_key and product_key are keys to dimension tables. They give the context. order_id only identifies the row.
units and revenue are additive: total units = 2 + 3 = 5 and total revenue = 1000 + 1200 = 2200.
unit_price is non-additive. Summing gives 500 + 400 = 900, which means nothing.
Overall average price = total revenue / total units = 2200 / 5 = 440. The plain average of the two prices is 450, which ignores the quantities.
examples.answer: Keys are dimension links; units and revenue are additive measures; unit_price is non-additive (use 2200 / 5 = 440).

examples.setup: End-of-month balance of one account over three months: 100, 120, 90. Can you add the balances across months?
steps: A balance is a snapshot at a moment, not an amount that accumulates.
Adding across accounts at one date is fine. Adding across months gives 100 + 120 + 90 = 310, which is not any balance.
Across time use the last value (90) or the average (310 / 3 = 103.33), depending on the question.
examples.answer: No. A balance is semi-additive: it adds across accounts but not across time.

cards.why: Knowing which column is the measure and which is a dimension decides what a query groups by and what it aggregates. In GATE: DA asks which of several columns is best stored as a measure, and which measures behave badly under SUM.
how: Look at each column and ask: do I sum it, or group by it?
Numeric facts you aggregate are measures; descriptive values you group by are dimension attributes.
Keys in the fact table point to dimension tables.
Check additivity before summing: ratios, prices and balances need care.
cards.mistake: Treating any number column as a measure. A zip code, a customer id or a year is a number, but you group by it and never sum it. Ask what the column describes: an event's size (measure) or its context (dimension).
edge_cases: Ids and codes stored as numbers are dimension attributes.
Counts of facts (COUNT(*)) are measures that need no column.
A year or month is a dimension attribute even though it is numeric.
Ratios are non-additive: store numerator and denominator separately.
connections: Measures roll up differently depending on their category (cards h5 to h7).
Fact and dimension tables, and the star schema, are covered in db.warehouse.
Foundations: **Sets and logic** (found.sets_logic): a dimension attribute names a set of possible values; a measure is a number you compute over a subset.

scenes.title: A location hierarchy built from the bottom up

steps.caption: Facts are stored per city. City is the finest level of the location dimension.
Mumbai and Pune belong to Maharashtra; Chennai and Madurai belong to Tamil Nadu. State is one level up.
Both states belong to India. Country is the next level up.
Each city has one state and each state one country: a single chain of parents, here Pune → Maharashtra → India.
Above Country sits ALL, one value meaning 'everything together'. Ignoring the dimension means grouping at ALL.

scenes.title: Roll-up, drill-down and slice on a small sales cube

steps.caption: Sales per item in thousand rupees: Laptop 70, Phone 50, Pen 5, Notebook 15.
Roll-up from Item to Type: add the children. Tech = 70 + 50 = 120, Office = 5 + 15 = 20. Four rows become two.
Drill-down from Type back to Item: Tech splits into Laptop 70 and Phone 50. Two rows become four.
Slice Type = Tech: keep only the Laptop and Phone rows. The level is still Item; only some values remain.
Roll-up: coarser and smaller. Drill-down: finer and bigger. Slice and dice: same level, fewer values.

set.text: judge by the level, not by the row count

scenes.title: Counting cuboids: one choice per dimension, then multiply

steps.caption: Time has 3 levels. A cuboid shows Time at one of them, or leaves it out (ALL): 3 + 1 = 4 choices.
Product has 2 levels: Item or Type, or ALL. That is 2 + 1 = 3 choices.
Store has one level, so Store or ALL: 1 + 1 = 2 choices.
A cuboid is one choice per dimension, for example (Month, Type, ALL). Every combination is a different cuboid.
Without hierarchies each dimension has one level and offers 2 choices, giving 2^3 = 8. Hierarchies multiply the choices.

scenes.title: Counting cells: values per axis, multiplied

steps.caption: Count the values at the chosen levels only: Type 3, Year 2, Region 2. Item, Quarter and City are not used.
Type gives 3 rows: A, B and C.
Year adds 2 columns: 3 × 2 = 6 cells in one layer.
Region adds 2 layers, East and West: 6 × 2 = 12 cells.
Total = 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 cells. The base cuboid (Item, Quarter, City) would have 6 × 8 × 4 = 192.

scenes.title: Which measures can be rebuilt from two partitions?

steps.caption: Split the data 1, 2, 4, 5, 9 into P1 = 2, 4, 9 and P2 = 1, 5. Can we rebuild the whole's answers from the pieces' answers?
SUM: 15 + 6 = 21, which equals the true sum. The same function on the pieces works: distributive.
MAX: the larger of 9 and 5 is 9, the true max. Distributive.
AVG: averaging 5 and 3 gives 4, not 4.2. Keep (sum, count) = (15, 3) and (6, 2): 21 / 5 = 4.2. Two numbers suffice: algebraic.
MEDIAN: the partial medians 4 and 3 cannot give the true median 4 (their average is 3.5). No fixed-size summary works: holistic.

scenes.title: Variance from stored (count, sum, sum of squares)

steps.caption: Cell X (values 2, 4, 9) stores (3, 15, 101). Cell Y (values 1, 5) stores (2, 6, 26). The raw values are gone.
Add the pieces across cells: n = 3 + 2 = 5, sum = 15 + 6 = 21, sum of squares = 101 + 26 = 127.
Mean = sum / count = 21 / 5 = 4.2.
Mean of squares = 127 / 5 = 25.4.
Variance = mean of squares − mean² = 25.4 − 17.64 = 7.76.
